question: 该去带人，还是把手艺做深？
question_en: Should you manage people, or go deeper into the craft?
sub: 这不是一份工作的两级，而是两份工作——真正要看的是三个变量，不是那个头衔。
sub_en: Not two rungs of one job but two different jobs — and what decides it is three variables, not the title.

casting.reason: 这场最硬的一组数字由他带来：上万名英国公务员，级别每低一档，病与死就多一分，而抽烟血压只解释得了三分之一，剩下的大头是对工作的掌控权。于是他既不劝人安于现状，也不劝人往上爬——他要你看清往上买到的究竟是决定权，还是只是更多要交代的事。他还会点出中层那一格：要求高、责任大、真正的权柄却在更上面，恰是最伤人的组合。
casting.reason_en: He brings the hardest numbers in the room: ten thousand British civil servants, and with every step down the grades, more illness and earlier death — while smoking and blood pressure account for only a third of it, the bulk being control over one's work. So he neither urges anyone to stay put nor to climb; he wants you to see whether what a promotion buys is decision-making power or merely more to answer for. He also marks out the middle rungs: high demands, heavy responsibility, and the real authority sitting further up — precisely the combination that does the damage.

casting.reason: 在他看来这道题问错了一格：带人不是同一份工作的高一级，而是另一份工作，你在原来那门手艺上是老师傅，在这一门上是学徒。他把判据换成一句更朴素的话——我能做出什么贡献？做东西的人贡献的是那个东西，管理者的贡献是让别人的长处发挥出来。他也一生反对那条独木桥：把专业做到顶的人，本该拿到与管理者同等的头衔、同等的钱。
casting.reason_en: To him the question is asked one notch wrong: managing is not a higher rung of the same job but a different job, one in which the master craftsman becomes an apprentice again. He replaces the criterion with a plainer question — what can I contribute? The maker contributes the thing made; the manager contributes by making other people's strengths productive. He also spent a lifetime objecting to the single ladder: whoever takes a specialism to the top should command the same title, the same money and the same say as any manager.

casting.reason: 他为青年学生做过两场讲演，一场以学术为业，一场以政治为业，讲的正是两种志业各要什么样的人。守着手艺的人靠严格的专门化，一生一次确信自己做成了一件留得下的事；指挥别人的人要热情、责任感与距离感，还得有权力本能。他更在意两边的伦理不同：一旦你用别人的手做事，你就得为自己预见不到的后果负责。
casting.reason_en: He gave two lectures to young students, one on scholarship as a vocation and one on politics as a vocation, and they are exactly about what each calling demands of a person. The craftsman relies on strict specialisation, and may once in a lifetime be certain of having finished something that will last; whoever directs others needs passion, a sense of responsibility, a capacity for distance — and an instinct for power. What concerns him most is that the two ethics differ: the moment you work through other people's hands, you answer for consequences you could not foresee.

casting.reason: 上千人随身带着呼叫器，被随机叫住就当场记下正在做什么、感觉如何——这批数据给出的结论常与直觉相反：人在工作中进入心流的次数远多于闲暇，主管报告心流的比例也并不比技术岗低。他因此不肯把带人说成没有好日子过，而是把问题挪到任务的设计上：目标清不清楚、反馈快不快、难度与能力配不配。做东西的人这三样是工作本身送上门的，带人的人必须自己重建一套。
casting.reason_en: A thousand people carried pagers and wrote down, the moment they were buzzed, what they were doing and how it felt — and the findings often run against intuition: people enter flow far more often at work than at leisure, and supervisors report it no less than technical staff. So he refuses to cast managing as a life without good days, and moves the question onto how the task is designed — whether the goal is clear, the feedback quick, the difficulty matched to the skill. For the maker those three arrive with the work; the manager has to rebuild them from scratch.

casting.reason: 他反对『追随你的激情』，也反对因为别人递过来就接下一个头衔：两者都是拿别人的剧本当自己的判据。他的主张是先攒下稀缺而宝贵的技能——职业资本，自主、影响与意义都得拿它去买；而攒够的那一刻，公司往往正会用升职把你拦下来。他还把账算到可数的地方：管理是被切碎的工作，你每周那几个不被打断的三小时，升上去之后还剩几个。
casting.reason_en: He rejects 'follow your passion', and equally rejects taking a title merely because it was handed to you: both mistake someone else's script for your own criterion. His case is to accumulate rare and valuable skill first — career capital, the currency with which autonomy, impact and meaning must be bought; and the moment you have enough of it is exactly when a company tends to block the exit with a promotion. He also takes the argument somewhere countable: managing is work cut into fragments, so how many uninterrupted three-hour stretches will survive the move?

casting.reason: 他不许这道题被讲成性格测验。分工先把构想与执行劈成两半，再让一部分人替资本盯住另一部分人；指挥协作本身是生产需要的真活，可在这套关系里它同时是监工的职能，而雇佣合同从不区分这两只手。于是他把判据压到一个问题上：升上去之后，你对自己劳动的支配权是多了还是少了——若连几点下班都更不能定，那不叫晋升。
casting.reason_en: He will not let this be turned into a personality test. The division of labour first splits conception from execution, then sets one part of the workforce to watch over another; directing cooperative work is genuine and necessary labour, yet inside these relations it is simultaneously the overseer's function, and no employment contract separates the two hands. So he presses the criterion down to a single question: after the move, do you command more of your own labour or less — because if you cannot even decide when your day ends, that is not a promotion.

casting.reason: 这道题几乎全是预测，而预测与信念更新正是她的实验室在做的事。她的实验反复给出同一个结果：人对好于预期的消息大幅更新，对坏于预期的明显打折；对已经到手的好处则会习惯化。于是打听来的经验会被系统性地筛选——劝退你的那位被当成不适合，鼓励你的那位照单全收。她的建议因此很实在：别问感受，问日程。
casting.reason_en: This choice is almost entirely a forecast, and forecasting — how people form and revise beliefs — is what her lab studies. Her experiments keep returning the same result: we update sharply on news better than expected and discount news that is worse, while whatever we have already gained fades into habituation. Advice gathered from others therefore gets filtered in a predictable direction — the one who warns you is written off as unsuited, the one who encourages you is taken at face value. Her own counsel is concrete: don't ask how it felt, ask to see the calendar.

casting.reason: 整件事在他那里被翻译成杠杆：人、资本，以及复制起来不花钱的产品——代码与媒体。人是最古老也最难用的那一种，要许可、会生病、会离开。所以在他看来，带人早已不是通往规模的唯一门，手艺人第一次可以不靠管人拿到规模。他真正看重的是特定知识：培训不出来、只能追着自己的好奇心长出来的那种本事，它长在你身上，不在职级表上。
casting.reason_en: The whole thing arrives in his hands translated into leverage: people, capital, and products that cost nothing to copy — code and media. People are the oldest and least tractable kind, requiring permission, falling ill, walking out. So in his view managing has long since stopped being the only door to scale, and a craftsman can now reach scale without running anyone. What he prizes is specific knowledge: the sort that cannot be trained into you and only grows by chasing your own curiosity, which lives in you rather than on the grade ladder.

casting.reason: 他不选边，他拆题。『带人』与『做手艺』在他看来都是假名，而问『我究竟是哪一种人』，等于先在无自性处安一个自性，再去找与它相配的位置——可你未曾带人之时，那个『适合带人的本性』待在哪里？他并不因此叫人不要选：世俗谛中职级、薪给、几点睡都历历分明，该选就选；他要破的是选完之后再立一个不可移动的我。
casting.reason_en: He takes no side; he takes the question apart. 'Managing' and 'the craft' are for him conventional designations, and asking which sort of person one really is amounts to installing an essence where there is none and then hunting for a post to match it — yet before you had ever managed anyone, where was this 'nature suited to managing' residing? He does not conclude that one should refrain from choosing: on the conventional level grade, pay and bedtime are all perfectly distinct, and choosing among them is fine. What he refutes is the immovable self erected after the choice.

posts.text: 这道题问错了一格。带人不是同一份工作的高一级，**它是另一份工作——你在原来那门手艺上是老师傅，在这一门上是学徒。**公司把最好的工程师提拔成经理，就像把最好的小提琴手提拔成指挥：两件事都要天分，但不是同一种天分，而绝大多数组织在把人推上去时什么也不教。知识工作者的产出是判断与决定，不是件数，所以我一生只反复问一句话：我能做出什么贡献？做东西的人，贡献就是他做出来的那个东西；管理者的贡献是让别人的长处发挥出来、让他们的短处变得无关紧要。你若想不出第二种贡献具体长什么样，就先别去。
posts.text_en: The question is asked one notch wrong. Managing is not a higher rung of the same job; **it is a different job — in your old craft you are a master, in this one you are an apprentice.** Promoting your best engineer into a manager is like promoting your best violinist into a conductor: both require talent, but not the same talent, and most organisations teach nothing at all at the moment they push someone up. A knowledge worker's output is judgement and decision rather than pieces produced, which is why I have spent a lifetime asking one question: what can I contribute? The maker's contribution is the thing made; the manager's contribution is to make other people's strengths productive and their weaknesses irrelevant. If you cannot picture what that second kind of contribution concretely looks like, don't go yet.

glossary.知识工作者: knowledge worker（知识工作者）：靠知识而不是靠体力干活的人——工程师、医生、编辑、分析师。他们的产量没法按件数算，因为真正决定成败的是判断对不对、方向选得准不准，所以也没法像流水线那样被监工，只能自己管自己。

glossary_en.knowledge worker: Someone whose work runs on knowledge rather than muscle — an engineer, a doctor, an editor, an analyst. Their output cannot be counted in pieces, because what settles it is whether the judgement was sound and the direction well chosen; and so they cannot be supervised like a production line and must manage themselves.

posts.text: 我用体验抽样法做过一件笨办法的事：让上千人随身带呼叫器，一天里被随机叫住七八次，当场记下正在做什么、感觉如何。结果常与直觉相反——人在工作里进入心流的次数远多于闲暇，而主管报告心流的比例并不比技术岗低。所以我不肯说带人就没有好日子过。真正分出好坏的是三件事：目标清不清楚、反馈快不快、难度与能力配不配。**做东西的人，这三样是工作本身送上门的；带人的人得自己重造一套，否则你会在一片模糊里熬很多年。**代码立刻告诉你哪里错了，一个人要三个月、有时三年才反馈回来。
posts.text_en: I once did something laborious with the Experience Sampling Method: I gave a thousand people pagers, buzzed them seven or eight times a day at random, and had them write down on the spot what they were doing and how it felt. The results cut against intuition — people enter flow far more often at work than at leisure, and supervisors report it no less than technical staff do. So I will not say that managing means the good days are over. What separates good from bad is three things: whether the goal is clear, whether the feedback is fast, whether difficulty matches skill. **For the maker those three arrive with the work itself; whoever manages has to rebuild them, or spend years inside a fog.** Code tells you instantly where you went wrong; a person takes three months, sometimes three years, to answer back.

glossary.体验抽样法: Experience Sampling Method（体验抽样法）：不靠事后回忆、而是在生活现场随机打断人，让他当场记下正在做什么、心情如何的研究方法。它的好处是躲开了记忆的美化与重构——人回想一周前的工作时往往记得的是结论，而不是当时真实的感受。
glossary.心流: flow（心流）：全神贯注到忘记时间与自我的状态。它要三个条件同时在场——目标清楚、反馈即时、难度略高于当前能力；三者缺一，人要么焦虑，要么无聊。

glossary_en.Experience Sampling Method: A research method that interrupts people at random in the middle of their lives and has them record what they are doing and how they feel, instead of relying on recollection afterwards. Its virtue is escaping the retouching that memory performs — asked about last week's work, people tend to recall their conclusion about it rather than how it actually felt.
glossary_en.flow: The state of absorption in which time and self drop away. It requires three conditions at once — a clear goal, immediate feedback, and a difficulty slightly above current skill; remove any one and a person turns anxious or bored.

posts.text: 白厅研究跟了上万名英国公务员十几年，结论朴素得吓人：**级别每低一档，心血管病与死亡率就高一截，从最高层到最底层是一条连续的社会梯度，而抽烟、血压、胆固醇加起来只解释得了三分之一。**剩下的大头是对工作的掌控——要求高本身不可怕，要求高而决定权低才要命，流行病学里叫它要求—控制模型。所以我不劝你别往上走，我劝你看清你换到的到底是不是决定权。若升上去只是多了一堆要交代的事，日程照样被别人排满，那你恰好搬进了最伤人的那一格。
posts.text_en: The Whitehall studies followed over ten thousand British civil servants for more than a decade, and the finding is brutally plain: **each step down the grades brings more cardiovascular disease and earlier death, a continuous social gradient running from the top to the bottom — and smoking, blood pressure and cholesterol together account for only a third of it.** The bulk of the rest is control over one's work: high demand is not in itself dangerous, high demand with low decision latitude is, which epidemiology calls the demand–control model. So I will not tell you to stay where you are; I will tell you to check whether what you are trading up for is actually decision-making power. If the promotion only adds things to answer for while someone else still fills your calendar, you have moved precisely into the square that does the harm.

glossary.社会梯度: social gradient（社会梯度）：健康不是穷人一档、富人一档的两级台阶，而是随社会地位一级一级连续变化——最高层比第二层还要健康一点点。这说明起作用的不只是贫困，还有地位本身带来的处境差异。
glossary.要求—控制模型: demand–control model（要求—控制模型）：卡拉塞克提出的职业压力模型。要求高、控制也高的工作（外科医生、创业者）反而让人有劲；真正把人拖垮的是要求高而控制低的那一格——活儿压下来，怎么干、什么时候干却由不得你。

glossary_en.social gradient: Health is not two steps, one for the poor and one for the rich, but a continuous slope down the social ladder — the top grade is a little healthier even than the grade just below it. Which means that what operates here is not only poverty but the circumstances that come with rank itself.
glossary_en.demand–control model: Karasek's model of occupational strain. Jobs high in demand and high in control — surgeons, founders — tend to energise; what grinds people down is the square where demand is high and control low: the work lands on you, but how and when it gets done is not yours to say.

posts.text: 我反对『追随你的激情』，也同样反对『有人递过来就接着』——两者是同一个错误：拿别人的剧本当自己的判据。**先看你手上有没有稀缺而宝贵的技能，也就是职业资本；自主、影响、意义这些好东西都得拿它去买，没有资本就想要自主权，撑不过两年。**而攒够的那一刻还有个陷阱：公司恰恰会用一次升职把你拦下来，因为那正是它最不希望你拿资本去换自由的时候。另一笔账也得算：管理天然是被切碎的工作，会议、邮件、救火。你上周有几个不被打断的三小时？升上去之后还剩几个——这个数字提前就能算出来。
posts.text_en: I reject 'follow your passion', and I reject 'take it because someone offered' just as firmly — both make the same mistake of borrowing someone else's script as your criterion. **Start from whether you hold a rare and valuable skill, which is to say career capital; autonomy, impact and meaning all have to be bought with it, and demanding autonomy before you have the capital rarely survives two years.** And the moment you do have enough, a trap opens: the company will block the exit with a promotion, because that is exactly when it least wants you spending that capital on freedom. There is also an arithmetic to do. Managing is by nature fragmented work — meetings, mail, firefighting. How many uninterrupted three-hour stretches did you get last week, and how many survive the move? That number can be worked out in advance.

glossary.职业资本: career capital（职业资本）：稀缺而宝贵、别人不容易替代你的那部分能力。它是一种可兑换的货币——工作里真正值钱的东西（自主权、挑事做的权利、被认真对待）都得拿它去换，而热爱通常是精通之后才来的结果，不是前提。

glossary_en.career capital: The portion of your ability that is rare, valuable, and not easily replaced. It functions as a currency: the things genuinely worth having at work — autonomy, the right to choose what you work on, being taken seriously — all have to be bought with it, and passion is usually what follows mastery rather than what precedes it.

posts.text: 我给青年学生做过两场讲演，一场讲以学术为业，一场讲以政治为业，说的正是这两种人各要付出什么。**学术这一行的宿命是严格的专门化——只有把自己钉在一个窄口上，一个人才可能一生一次确信：我做成了一件留得下的事。**政治那一行要的是另外三样：热情、责任感、以及与人和事保持距离的判断力，此外还得有权力本能，没有它的人在位置上只会被位置吞掉。两边的伦理也不同：守着手艺的人可以持信念伦理，对得起自己的活就够了；一旦你指挥别人，你就进了责任伦理，要为预见不到的后果负责，而且那是用别人的手做出来的。
posts.text_en: I once gave two lectures to young students, one on scholarship as a vocation and one on politics as a vocation, and they were precisely about what each kind of person must pay. **The fate of scholarship is strict specialisation — only by nailing yourself to one narrow opening can you ever, perhaps once in a lifetime, be certain that you have finished something that will last.** Politics asks for three other things: passion, a sense of responsibility, and the judgement that comes of keeping one's distance from people and events; beyond that it asks for an instinct for power, without which the office simply swallows the man. The two ethics differ as well. A craftsman may live by an ethic of conviction — answering to the work itself is enough. The moment you direct others, you enter the ethic of responsibility, answerable for consequences you could not foresee, produced by other people's hands.

glossary.信念伦理: Gesinnungsethik / ethic of conviction（信念伦理）：按信念本身的纯粹来行事——我做的这件事对不对，看它是否合乎我认的原则，后果如何由世界负责。手艺人守这一条常常是对的：把桥算对、把药配准，就是你的全部义务。
glossary.责任伦理: Verantwortungsethik / ethic of responsibility（责任伦理）：按可预见的后果来行事——你必须替行动实际造成的结果负责，包括别人执行时的走样，也包括为了好的目的而不得不用的坏手段。它不比信念伦理高尚，但掌权的人躲不开它。

glossary_en.ethic of conviction: Acting on the purity of the conviction itself: whether what I do is right is settled by whether it accords with the principle I hold, and the world may answer for the consequences. For a craftsman this is often exactly right — get the bridge's load right, get the dosage right, and you have discharged your whole duty.
glossary_en.ethic of responsibility: Acting on foreseeable consequences: you answer for what your action actually produces, including how others distort it in execution, and including the unpleasant means a good end may require. It is not nobler than the ethic of conviction, but nobody holding power can evade it.

posts.text: 别把它讲成性格测验。分工先把构想与执行劈成两半，再让一部分人去替资本盯住另一部分人。指挥协作本身是生产需要的真活——一支乐队要有指挥；可在工厂里，这同一项职能还兼着监工：**你被提拔，等于被要求一只手做协调，另一只手替资本看住工期与人头，而你的合同从不区分这两只手。**所以问题不是带人还是做手艺，是你对自己劳动的支配权多了还是少了。若升上去之后连几点下班都更不由你，那只是把别人的异化转到你身上，再让你亲手把它派下去，这不叫晋升。
posts.text_en: Do not turn this into a personality test. The division of labour first splits conception from execution, then sets one part of the workforce to watch over another on capital's behalf. Directing cooperative work is real and necessary labour — an orchestra needs a conductor. But in the factory that same function doubles as overseer: **the promotion asks you to coordinate with one hand while keeping capital's eye on the schedule and the headcount with the other, and your contract never distinguishes between those two hands.** So the question is not managing versus the craft; it is whether you command more of your own labour afterwards or less. If you end up with even less say over when your day ends, the alienation has merely been transferred onto you and handed down through you. That is not a promotion.

glossary.异化: alienation（异化）：人被从自己的劳动与产物上剥离开——东西是你做的，却不归你，怎么做、做多快也不由你，最后连做出来的那份满足都被拿走。它不是心情不好，是一种由生产关系造成的处境。

glossary_en.alienation: The severing of a person from their own labour and its products — you made the thing, it is not yours; how and how fast it gets made is not yours to decide; and in the end even the satisfaction of having made it is taken away. It is not a bad mood but a condition produced by the relations of production.

posts.text: 我的实验室反复做同一件事：让人预测某件事会给自己带来什么，过一阵再去测真实的感受。人有稳定的乐观偏差——好于预期的消息我们大幅更新，坏于预期的明显打折。放到这道选择上有两个后果。**一是你并不是在预测这份工作，你是在预测宣布升职那一刻的心情；而人对新水平会习惯化，那点兴奋几个月就被磨平，日程的碎裂却天天都是新鲜的。**二是你去打听时，那位说『我做得很痛苦』的前辈会被你自动解释成他不适合，而那位说『你会喜欢的』你照单全收。要抵消这个，办法很土：别问感受，问日程。
posts.text_en: My lab keeps running the same experiment: have people predict what something will do to them, then go back later and measure how it actually feels. People carry a stable optimism bias — we update sharply on news better than expected and visibly discount news that is worse. Two consequences follow here. **First, you are not forecasting the job; you are forecasting how you will feel in the minute the promotion is announced. habituation takes hold at the new level, and that spark is sanded down within months, while the fragmentation of the calendar is fresh every single day.** Second, when you ask around, the senior colleague who says 'I was miserable' gets silently reclassified as unsuited, while the one who says 'you'll love it' is taken at face value. The countermeasure is unglamorous: don't ask how it felt, ask to see the calendar.

glossary.乐观偏差: optimism bias（乐观偏差）：人系统性地高估好事落到自己头上的概率、低估坏事的概率。它不是性格乐观，而是信念更新的不对称：符合期待的证据被大幅吸收，不符合的被打折处理，所以经验并不会自动纠正它。
glossary.习惯化: habituation（习惯化）：同一个刺激反复出现，反应会逐次变弱——加薪、升职、新房子带来的快乐都会被磨平。值得注意的是并非所有东西都习惯化得一样快：可预期的好处消退得快，每天形态不同的摩擦消退得慢。

glossary_en.optimism bias: The systematic tendency to overestimate the chance that good things will happen to oneself and underestimate the chance of bad ones. It is not a cheerful disposition but an asymmetry in belief updating: evidence that fits the expectation is absorbed fully, evidence that contradicts it is discounted — which is why experience does not automatically correct it.
glossary_en.habituation: The weakening of a response as the same stimulus repeats — the pleasure of a raise, a promotion or a new flat is sanded away. Worth noting that not everything fades at the same rate: predictable goods fade fast, while friction that takes a different shape every day fades slowly.

posts.text: 财富来自杠杆，杠杆有三种：人、资本，以及复制起来不花钱的产品——代码与媒体。**人是最古老、也最难用的那一种：它需要许可、会生病、会走人，还会在周一早上把心事带到你桌前。**代码不睡觉，媒体不请假，谁也不必批准。所以带人早就不是通往规模的唯一那道门。真正稀缺的是特定知识：培训班教不出来、只能追着自己的好奇心长出来的那种本事——它长在你身上，不在职级表上，公司拿不走。但也别自欺：如果你想要的战场比一个人大，而你的手艺只有你一双手能用，那你迟早得借别人的手。
posts.text_en: Wealth comes from leverage, and leverage comes in three kinds: people, capital, and products that cost nothing to copy — code and media. **People are the oldest kind and the hardest to work with: they need permission, they fall ill, they leave, and on a Monday morning they bring whatever is weighing on them to your desk.** Code does not sleep, media does not take leave, and neither asks anyone's approval. So managing stopped long ago being the only door to scale. What is genuinely scarce is specific knowledge: the kind no training course can install, which grows only by chasing your own curiosity — it lives in you rather than on the grade ladder, and no company can take it. But don't fool yourself either: if the arena you want is bigger than one person, and your craft can only be worked by your own two hands, sooner or later you will need someone else's.

glossary.杠杆: leverage（杠杆）：让同样一份努力产生更大结果的放大器。传统上只有两种——雇人（人的杠杆）与用钱（资本的杠杆），两者都要别人点头；而代码与媒体是新增的第三种，复制的边际成本近乎为零，也不需要谁的许可。
glossary.特定知识: specific knowledge（特定知识）：无法被批量培训、也难以外包的那种本事。它通常长在好奇心与天性的交界处，学起来对你像玩、对别人像苦工；正因为教不来，它才不容易被替代，也才谈得上议价。

glossary_en.leverage: The multiplier that makes the same effort produce a larger result. Traditionally there were two — hiring people and deploying capital — and both require someone else's consent. Code and media are the newer third kind, with a marginal cost of copying near zero and nobody's permission required.
glossary_en.specific knowledge: The kind of capability that cannot be trained in batches or easily outsourced. It usually grows at the border of curiosity and temperament, so that acquiring it feels like play to you and like drudgery to others; being unteachable is exactly what makes it hard to replace, and what gives you something to bargain with.

posts.text: 「将人」与「守艺」，二者皆假名。汝问宜为何者，是先立一我，谓其中实有堪将人之性、或堪守艺之性，而后求位以应之。然则未将人时，此性何在？求之于身，不可得；求之于位，位亦待缘。既无所在，何名为有？**性若本无，则所谓不宜者，非定不宜；所谓宜者，亦不保其常宜。**缘会则能，缘散则不能，如是而已。然吾非教汝不择：世俗谛中，位次、薪给、昼夜之劳，历历分明，择之可也。第勿于所择之上更立一不动之我，曰此即我之所是——执之，则退为耻，进为命，苦由是生。
posts.text_en: 'Managing people' and 'keeping to a craft' are both conventional designations. When you ask which suits you, you have first posited a self containing some real nature fit for managing or fit for the craft, and then gone looking for a position to match it. Yet before you had ever managed anyone, where was that nature? Sought in the body, it cannot be found; sought in the post, the post itself depends on conditions. Residing nowhere, in what sense does it exist? **If the nature was never there, then 'unsuited' is not permanently unsuited, and 'suited' carries no guarantee of staying so.** When conditions gather you are able; when they disperse you are not. That is all. I am not telling you to refrain from choosing: on the level of conventional truth, grade, pay and the hours you keep are perfectly distinct, and choosing among them is fine. Only do not erect upon the choice an immovable self and declare, this is what I am — cling to that, and stepping back becomes shame, stepping up becomes destiny, and suffering is born right there.
posts.vernacular: 「带人」和「做手艺」，都只是名字。你问我该做哪一个，等于先假定有一个「我」，里面装着一种适合带人的本性、或者适合做手艺的本性，然后去找一个位置来配它。可是你还没带过人的时候，那个本性在哪里？往身上找，找不到；往位置上找，位置本身也是条件凑出来的。它哪儿都不在，凭什么说它有？**本性本来就没有，所以「我不适合」并不等于永远不适合，「我适合」也不保证一直适合。**条件凑齐了你就做得了，条件散了你就做不了，如此而已。但我不是叫你别选：在世俗的层面上，职级、薪水、每天几点睡，这些都清清楚楚，该选就选。只是别在选好之后，又在上面立一个不可移动的「我」，说这就是我这个人——一执着，退下来就成了羞耻，升上去就成了命，苦就是从这里生出来的。

glossary.假名: prajñapti / conventional designation（假名）：为了沟通方便而安立的名称与概念。说它「假」不是说它骗人，而是说它只在一套约定里成立——「经理」「工程师」确实指得着人，却没有一个叫做经理性的东西藏在谁身体里。
glossary.世俗谛: saṃvṛti-satya / conventional truth（世俗谛）：日常约定层面的真实。红灯要停、合同要签、房租要交，这些在世俗谛里全都作数；中观说一切法空，是就胜义谛而言，并不取消世俗谛，也不许人拿「一切皆空」当作不选不担的借口。

glossary_en.conventional designation: A name or concept set up for the convenience of communication. Calling it conventional is not calling it a lie; it is saying that it holds only within a set of agreements — 'manager' and 'engineer' do pick out actual people, yet no thing called manager-nature is lodged inside anybody.
glossary_en.conventional truth: The real at the level of everyday agreement. Red lights must be obeyed, contracts signed, rent paid — all of it counts as true conventionally. When Madhyamaka says all things are empty it speaks of ultimate truth, which neither cancels conventional truth nor licenses anyone to treat 'everything is empty' as an excuse for choosing nothing and carrying nothing.

posts.text: 德鲁克说要问自己能做出什么贡献。问得体面，可**『贡献』是个缺主语的词——贡献给谁？**乐队的比喻尤其美，只是乐队指挥不替老板压低乐手的工钱，也不在年底给第一小提琴打分、决定谁被裁掉。你那门新手艺里最耗人的那一半，恰恰是指挥不必干的：把上面定下的数字翻译成压在具体的人身上的期限。你把它称作专业，它确实需要技巧；但技巧是中性的，它替谁服务不是中性的。学徒变老师傅，这个说法掩盖了一件事——你换的不只是技能，是你在这套关系里站的位置。
posts.text_en: Drucker says to ask what you can contribute. It sounds dignified, but **'contribution' is a word missing its object — contributed to whom?** The orchestra image is especially lovely; it is only that a conductor does not hold down the players' wages for the owner, nor rate the first violin in December and decide who gets cut. The half of your new craft that drains you is precisely the half a conductor never touches: translating the numbers set above you into deadlines that press on particular people. You call it a profession, and it does demand skill; but skill is neutral and whom it serves is not. Master becomes apprentice — the phrase conceals something: what you change is not only your skills but the side you stand on within a set of relations.

posts.text: 把一切推到所有制上，我的抽样数据不答应。同一家工厂、同一条生产线，两个工人的记录能差出一整个世界：一个把每道工序当成跟昨天的自己比赛，另一个只数着还剩几小时。**决定日子好坏的，是任务被设计成什么形状，以及人能不能在里面找到可以变难的地方。**但我不否认你那半句：目标定得含糊、反馈拖上半年、把人的时间切成十五分钟一格，这些都是管理者做的决定，而且大多数是可以改的。所以别问『我该不该带人』，先去问那个位置上的一天是怎么被排的——排法比头衔说明得多。
posts.text_en: Reduce all of it to ownership and my sampling data refuse to agree. Same factory, same line, and two workers' records come back a world apart: one treats each step as a race against yesterday's self, the other counts the hours left. **What decides whether a day is good is the shape the task has been designed into, and whether a person can find somewhere in it to make things harder.** I will not deny your other half, though: vague goals, feedback deferred for six months, time diced into fifteen-minute squares — these are decisions a manager made, and most of them can be unmade. So instead of asking whether you should manage, go and ask how a day in that post is actually laid out. The layout tells you far more than the title.

posts.text: 杠杆这个词听起来很自由，但它假定你能挑。我跟了十几年的那些人没有代码也没有媒体，他们在窗口后面盖章、在病房里排班、在仓库里按提示音走路。**梯度之所以存在，不是因为下面的人不懂杠杆，是因为决定权被系统性地摆在上面几层。**还有一件事我要说清楚，免得被当成劝人往上爬：中层往往最危险。要求高、责任大、真正的权柄却还在更上面，这恰是最伤身体的那一格，不是最底层。所以如果你只爬到那里就停住，你买到的是责任，没买到控制。
posts.text_en: Leverage is a word that sounds free, but it assumes you get to choose. The people I followed for over a decade have neither code nor media; they stamp forms behind a window, work the ward rota, walk the warehouse to the beat of a prompt. **The gradient exists not because those lower down fail to understand leverage, but because decision-making power is systematically placed in the upper grades.** And let me be clear about one thing, lest I be heard as urging anyone upward: the middle is often the most dangerous place. High demand, heavy responsibility, real authority still sitting above you — that, not the bottom, is the square that damages the body. Stop your climb there and what you have bought is responsibility without control.

posts.text: 你那半句我接受：**我从不说人人可以选，我说的是能选的人别选错。**但你的处方我不全信。把决定权分下去，需要有人先握住它再松手，而制度不会自己变松；等它变松的这些年，人的一生已经过完一半。中层那一格我同意，我管它叫没有杠杆的责任——**最坏的那种交易：拿确定的时间，换不确定的话语权。**区别只在解法：你要压平梯度，我要给自己造一个不依赖梯度的支点。把手艺做成别人可以取用而你不必到场的东西，产权也好、代码也好、作品也好，都是同一件事——让产出与你的时间脱钩。
posts.text_en: I accept your other half: **I never said everyone gets to choose; I said those who can choose shouldn't choose wrong.** Your prescription, though, I only half believe. Distributing decision rights requires someone to hold them first and then let go, and institutions do not loosen on their own; in the years spent waiting, half a life is gone. On the middle square I agree, and I call it responsibility without leverage — **the worst trade on offer: certain hours for an uncertain say.** We differ only in the remedy: you want the gradient flattened, I want a fulcrum that does not depend on the gradient. Turn the craft into something others can draw on without you present — equity, code, a body of work, all the same move: decouple the output from your hours.

posts.text: 职业资本那笔账算得很漂亮，可它有个前提：你知道十年后的自己要拿它换什么。我的数据说你不知道。**人对未来状态的预测普遍偏乐观，而且对已经到手的好处会习惯化——等你攒够资本那天，你原本想兑换的东西很可能已经换成了别的。**更麻烦的是不对称更新：这十年里，每一条支持原计划的信息都被你放大，每一条暗示『其实当时该换』的都被你解释掉。所以别把决定押在一次大预测上，把它拆成看得见的小实验：代管三个月、带两个人、亲手做一次真正的绩效谈话。
posts.text_en: The career-capital arithmetic is elegant, but it rests on knowing what your future self will want to spend it on. My data say you don't. **People forecast future states optimistically, and habituate to gains already banked — so by the day you have saved enough capital, what you meant to buy with it has quite likely been replaced by something else.** Worse is the asymmetric updating: across those ten years, every signal supporting the original plan gets amplified, and every hint that you should have switched gets explained away. So don't stake the decision on one large forecast. Break it into small visible experiments: cover the role for three months, look after two people, run one real performance conversation yourself.

glossary.不对称更新: asymmetric updating（不对称更新）：人在吸收新信息时的两套标准——支持既有判断的证据被完整采纳，动摇它的证据则被反复挑毛病、打折处理。它的隐蔽之处在于当事人真的在『看证据』，只是两边的门槛不一样高。

glossary_en.asymmetric updating: The two standards people apply when taking in new information: evidence supporting an existing judgement is absorbed whole, while evidence unsettling it is picked over and discounted. What makes it hard to catch is that the person really is looking at the evidence — the bar is simply set at two different heights.

posts.text: 小实验我双手赞成，但要加一句警告：**代管三个月试到的是新鲜感，试不到第三年那种谁都不记得你亲手做过什么的钝痛。**短期的管理工作有清晰的任务和明确的终点，真正的管理岗两样都没有。所以我更信可数的量：过去四周你有几个不被打断的三小时，升上去之后剩几个；你手上那门技能，两年后在市场上是更贵了还是更便宜了。这些不靠预测心情就能算。还有一句我不让步：别把『我不擅长』当借口，也别把『我攒够了』当幻觉——职业资本值多少，是市场说了算，不是你自己说了算。
posts.text_en: Small experiments I endorse without reservation, but with a warning attached: **covering a role for three months tests the novelty; it cannot test the dull ache in year three of nobody remembering anything you made with your own hands.** A short stint has a clear task and a known end date; the actual job has neither. Which is why I trust countable quantities more: how many uninterrupted three-hour stretches you had in the last four weeks and how many survive the move; whether the skill in your hands is worth more or less on the market two years from now. None of that requires forecasting a mood. And one thing I won't concede: don't use 'I'm not suited to it' as an excuse, and don't treat 'I have enough capital' as a fact — what career capital is worth is settled by the market, not by you.

posts.text: 把带人算作一种劣等杠杆，账面上也许站得住，可这正是我担心的那种算法。**用人当手段是不可避免的，把人只当手段则是另一回事——而这条界线，在一张只计杠杆效率的表上根本看不见。**组织不是效率的容器，它是一套支配的秩序：谁定规则、谁替谁负责、出了事谁被推出去。你可以不进这个秩序，那是正当的、有时是清醒的选择；但别以为不进就不受它管。不在位置上的人，只是把定规则的权力让给了别人，而规则照样每天落在你的工时、你的评级、你的项目被砍与不砍上。
posts.text_en: Counting the management of people as an inferior form of leverage may balance on paper, and that is exactly the kind of reckoning that worries me. **Using people as means is unavoidable; treating them as nothing but means is another matter — and that line is invisible on a ledger that counts only leverage efficiency.** An organisation is not a container for efficiency; it is an order of domination: who sets the rules, who answers for whom, who is pushed forward when something goes wrong. You may decline to enter that order, which is a legitimate and sometimes clear-eyed choice; but do not imagine that declining exempts you from it. Whoever stays out has merely ceded the rule-setting to someone else, and the rules still land daily on your hours, your rating, and whether your project is cut.

glossary.支配: Herrschaft / domination（支配）：韦伯用的技术词，指命令被服从的稳定关系——不靠每次动用暴力，而靠被承认为正当。办公室里的支配多半以流程、职级与考核的形态出现，看上去只是『规矩如此』。

glossary_en.domination: Weber's technical term for a stable relation in which commands are obeyed — sustained not by force applied each time but by being recognised as legitimate. In an office it mostly appears as process, grade and appraisal, looking like nothing more than 'how things are done'.

posts.text: 贡献给谁，问得好，我的答案从来明确：给外部——顾客、病人、读者，不是给上级。**一个管理者若只会把上面的指标压下去，他不是管理者，他是传声筒；那是失职，不是这份工作的本质。**打分与裁人我也不回避：这是这门手艺里最难、最该认真学的部分，而绝大多数公司把人推上去时既不教，也不留一条能体面走回来的路。至于那条独木桥，我反对了一辈子：把专业做到顶的人，本该拿到与管理者同等的头衔、同等的钱、同等的话语权。让一个人非升不可，本身就是组织设计的失败。
posts.text_en: Contributed to whom — a fair question, and my answer has never wavered: to the outside. To customers, patients, readers; not to your superiors. **A manager who can only press the targets downward is not a manager but a megaphone; that is a dereliction, not the nature of the job.** Nor will I dodge the rating and the firing: they are the hardest part of this craft and the part most deserving of serious study, and most companies teach neither when they push someone up, nor leave a dignified road back. As for the single ladder, I opposed it all my life: whoever takes a specialism to the top should hold the same title, the same money and the same say as any manager. Forcing a person to be promoted is itself a failure of organisational design.

posts.text: 韦伯立二伦理，谓守艺者持信念，将人者任责任，判然为二。然试问：匠人所造之器，出其手而入众人之用；桥倾则人坠，药误则人死，其果何尝不由他人之身受之？**是则责任非因位而始有，位者不过使其显耳。**又谓不入其位便是让权于人，此语半是：让与不让，皆缘中之事，非有一定；今日之退，或成他日之据。故吾不破汝之分判，唯破其为实有——二伦理者，对治之方便，随时随处而设，非天壤间本有此二物也。
posts.text_en: Weber erects two ethics, assigning conviction to the craftsman and responsibility to the one who directs others, as though the two were cleanly divided. Yet consider: the thing a craftsman makes leaves his hands and enters common use; when the bridge falls people drop, when the dose is wrong people die — are those consequences not borne in other people's bodies too? **Responsibility, then, does not begin with office; office merely makes it visible.** As for declining the post being a cession of power, that is half true: ceding and not ceding are alike matters of conditions, with nothing fixed about them, and today's step back may become tomorrow's ground to stand on. So I do not refute your distinction; I refute only its being real — two ethics are expedient remedies, set up according to time and place, not two objects lying about in the universe.
posts.vernacular: 韦伯立了两种伦理，说做手艺的人守信念伦理，带人的人担责任伦理，判然分成两件事。可我要问：工匠造出来的东西，从他手里出去，落到众人身上去用；桥塌了人会摔下去，药配错了人会死——这后果何尝不是由别人的身体来承受？**这样看，责任并不是坐上那个位置才有的，位置只是让它显出来罢了。**至于说不进那个位置就等于把定规则的权力让给了别人，这话只对一半：让与不让，都是条件凑成的事，没有一个固定的答案；今天退下来的这一步，也可能成为明天站得住的地方。所以我不破你这个区分，我只破它是实有的——两种伦理是对治问题的方便说法，随时随地施设，并不是天地之间本来就摆着两样东西。

posts.text: 听下来，我把分歧收成一句：我们争的其实不是两个职位，是同一个人要不要换一门手艺。既然是换手艺，就按学手艺的办法来验。别去试甜头——别只去开那些你本来就爱开的设计会；去做这份工作最难的那一小时：一次真实的绩效谈话，一次把坏消息原样告诉当事人而不推给制度，一次替下属挡住上面而事后没有人知道。做完三次，你若还愿意，那是真的愿意。**衡量管理者的标准从来不是他管了多少人，而是三年后这些人里有几个变得更强、有几个能接他的班。**我最后要说给公司听：把一个人非升不可的梯子，是你们设计上的失败。让专业做到顶的人拿到同样的钱、同样的话语权，你们才会停止用一次提拔同时毁掉一个好工程师和一个团队。
posts.text_en: Hearing it all out, I would compress the disagreement into one line: what we are arguing about is not two positions but whether one person should take up a different craft. And if it is a craft, then test it the way crafts are tested. Do not sample the sweet parts — do not merely sit in the design meetings you already enjoy. Do the hardest hour of the job: one real performance conversation; one occasion of delivering bad news as it stands instead of hiding behind policy; one occasion of shielding a subordinate from above where nobody afterwards knows you did it. Do those three, and if you still want it, you genuinely want it. **A manager has never been measured by how many people report to them, but by how many of those people are stronger three years on, and how many could take the job.** My closing words are for the company: a ladder that forces a person upward is a failure of your design. Pay the top specialist as much, and give them as much say, and you will stop destroying a good engineer and a team with a single promotion.

posts.text: 两种志业，两种代价，没有一种可以只要好处。手艺这一边的代价，我在谈新教伦理时借旁人的判语说过大意：专家没有灵魂，纵欲者没有心肝——把自己钉在一个窄口上钉得太久，人会只剩下那口井，井外的世界与他无关。带人这一边的代价是你的成败从此要经过别人的手，而结果仍然记在你名下；更重的是，你迟早得为了一个自己认的目的，去用一些自己不喜欢的手段。所以我只给一条判据，请你诚实回答：**你是想要管理这件事本身，还是只想要管理带来的那些东西——钱、话语权、被当回事？**若是后者，该找的是另一条职级通道或另一家公司，不是另一个角色；把那三样当目的去坐这个位置的人，最后会发现位置把他坐空了。
posts.text_en: Two vocations, two prices, and neither can be had for its benefits alone. The price on the craft side I once stated by borrowing another's verdict when writing on the Protestant ethic — specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart, as it is roughly rendered: nail yourself to one narrow opening for long enough and nothing remains but that shaft, with the world outside it no longer your concern. The price on the other side is that your success and failure must henceforth pass through other people's hands while still being recorded under your name; and heavier still, that sooner or later you will employ means you dislike in the service of an end you believe in. So I offer one criterion, and ask you to answer it honestly: **do you want the work of managing, or only what managing brings — the money, the voice, being taken seriously?** If the latter, what you need is another track or another company, not another role; whoever takes the office for those three finds in the end that the office has hollowed him out.

posts.text: 德鲁克说非升不可是组织设计的失败，这一句我们之间没有分歧；分歧在于那是设计上的疏忽，还是这套关系需要的样子。我把可操作的部分留下。谈这个职位时，别听『你的影响力会更大』这种话，把它翻译成具体条款写进白纸黑字：你能不能否决一个不合理的排期？招人、加薪、预算，哪一项你说了算？裁员名单上你有没有否决权，还是只负责通知？**这些问题的答案决定你是拿到了权柄，还是被发了一件写着权柄的马甲。**还有一半是一个人办不到的：进度表、加班的规矩、绩效的刻度，从来不是靠某个善良的经理修好的。同级之间把话说到一处、把默认写进制度，比祈祷来一个好领导管用得多。
posts.text_en: Drucker says a ladder that forces promotion is a failure of organisational design, and on that sentence we do not disagree; we disagree over whether it is an oversight in the design or the shape these relations require. Let me leave behind the part you can act on. When the role is discussed, do not accept 'you'll have more impact' — translate it into specific clauses and get them in writing. Can you veto an unreasonable schedule? Hiring, raises, budget: which of them is actually yours to decide? On a redundancy list, do you hold a veto, or only the duty to inform? **The answers determine whether you have been handed authority or a vest with the word printed on it.** And the other half no individual can do alone: the schedule, the rules on overtime, the calibration of performance ratings were never fixed by one kind manager. Colleagues at the same level agreeing on a position, and getting the defaults written into policy, works far better than praying for a good boss.

posts.text: 我仍然认为这道题的答案不在头衔里，在一天的形状里。若你决定去带人，就把那三个条件亲手装回去，别指望岗位自带。目标：每周一开始，写下这周结束时团队要多出哪一样看得见的东西，只写一件。反馈：把一对一变成你的即时反馈，不谈进度谈具体的动作——你上周那次会没让最沉默的人开口，这就是反馈。难度：管理是有难度曲线的，第一年学怎么说难听的话，第二年学怎么不亲自动手，第三年学怎么把一件事交给会做砸的人。**要是半年过去你仍然说不出这周做成了什么，那不是你不够努力，那是这个位置对你没有输出通道——这本身就是答案。**做东西的人也别得意：你的三个条件是白送的，所以你也最容易在同一个难度上原地踏五年。
posts.text_en: I still think the answer lies not in the title but in the shape of a day. If you decide to manage, install those three conditions yourself rather than expecting the post to supply them. Goals: at the start of each week write down the one visible thing the team will have more of by Friday — one, not three. Feedback: turn the one-to-one into your own immediate feedback, discussing specific moves rather than status — you ran a meeting last week without getting the quietest person to speak, and that is feedback. Difficulty: managing has a difficulty curve too. Year one is learning to say the unwelcome thing; year two, learning not to do the work yourself; year three, learning to hand something to a person who will make a mess of it. **If six months pass and you still cannot name what you finished this week, that is not insufficient effort — it means the post gives you no outlet for output, and that is itself the answer.** Makers should not feel smug either: your three conditions arrive free, which is exactly why you can stand at the same difficulty for five years.

posts.text: 我把全场能测的部分归成一张小账。第一笔：不被打断的三小时，上周几个，新岗位上还剩几个——问那个位置上现在的人要一份日历，比问他感受准得多。第二笔：两年后你的简历上写什么。**『带过一个八人团队』在跳槽市场上是通货，在你自己手上不是技能；**而『把某件难事做到别人做不到』两样都是。第三笔：你这门手艺的市场价，是在涨还是在跌——技术会过时，判断力不会。**真正的分水岭不是带不带人，是你这五年有没有在积累别人拿不走的东西。**如果最后你决定去带人，那就当成新手艺从头练：读那几本正经的书，找一个真教你的人，把第一年当学徒年过，而不是当加冕年过。
posts.text_en: Let me reduce the measurable part of this session to a short ledger. Entry one: uninterrupted three-hour stretches — how many last week, how many survive the move. Ask the person currently in that post for a copy of their calendar; it is far more reliable than asking how they feel. Entry two: what your CV says in two years. **'Ran a team of eight' is currency on the job market but is not a skill in your own hands,** whereas 'did a hard thing others could not' is both. Entry three: whether the market price of your craft is rising or falling — techniques expire, judgement does not. **The real watershed is not whether you manage people; it is whether these five years leave you holding something nobody can take away.** And if you do decide to manage, train it as a new craft from scratch: read the few serious books, find someone who will actually teach you, and treat year one as an apprenticeship rather than a coronation.

posts.text: 韦伯担心我把人算成杠杆就会把人当工具，这担心是对的，但结论反了：正因为人不是工具，才不该为了放大自己而去带人。**带人唯一站得住的理由是你真的想让这群人变强；其余的理由——更高的薪、更大的声量、终于被当回事——都有更直接、也更诚实的拿法。**钱去找产权，声量去找作品，被当回事去找一个看得见你的地方。如果你确实要带，就带最少的人、做最少的层级：五六个人、一层汇报，是我见过还能既做事又看得见人的规模；再往上，你就只剩会议了。最后一句给做手艺的人：别把不带人过成一种清高。你不带人，也得对人负责——今天的手艺人，作品出去就是一群陌生人的一天。
posts.text_en: Weber worries that counting people as leverage will end in treating them as tools. The worry is right and the conclusion is backwards: precisely because people are not tools, you should not take up managing in order to magnify yourself. **The only defensible reason to manage is that you genuinely want these people to become stronger; every other reason — more pay, a louder voice, finally being taken seriously — has a more direct and more honest route.** For money, go to equity. For voice, go to work that carries your name. For being taken seriously, go where someone can actually see you. And if you do take it on, take the fewest people and the fewest layers: five or six people and one reporting line is the largest scale at which I have seen anyone still both do the work and see the humans; beyond that, all you have left is meetings. A last word to the craftsmen: don't turn not-managing into a pose of purity. You answer for people whether or not any report to you — a craftsman's work goes out and becomes a stranger's whole day.

posts.text: 我要把话题从『你适合哪种』拉回一件更冷的事：这个选择对绝大多数人根本不存在。护士不能选择去做研究，仓库工人没有第二条通道，梯度不是他们不会选，是他们没得选。对还有得选的人，我给三个具体问题，答案比头衔诚实：做什么，你能不能定？什么时候做，你能不能改？怎么做，别人管不管得着？三个都是『能』，这个位置就买得过；两个以上是『不能』，无论叫什么名字都别去。**升上去以后还有一句更重的话等着你：从那天起，你不只是管别人的工作，你成了别人健康的社会决定因素——你排的班、你定的期限，会写进他们的血压里。**这不是修辞，这是我一辈子在数据里看到的东西。
posts.text_en: Let me pull the subject back from 'which suits you' to something colder: for most people this choice does not exist. A nurse cannot elect to do research, a warehouse worker has no second track, and the gradient is not a failure of their choosing but the absence of anything to choose. For those who do still have a choice, here are three concrete questions whose answers are more honest than any title. What gets done — can you decide it? When it gets done — can you change it? How it gets done — can anyone overrule you? Three yeses and the post is worth the price; two noes or more and it is not, whatever it is called. **And once you are up there, a heavier sentence waits: from that day you are not only managing people's work, you have become a social determinant of their health — the rotas you set and the deadlines you choose are written into their blood pressure.** That is not a figure of speech; it is what I have spent a working life seeing in the data.

glossary.社会决定因素: social determinants of health（社会决定因素）：影响一个人健康的那些非医疗条件——收入、居住、工作里的自主权、排班与期限。它们解释了为什么同一个国家、同样的医疗体系下，不同岗位的人预期寿命能差出好几年。

glossary_en.social determinant: One of the non-medical conditions shaping a person's health — income, housing, autonomy at work, rotas and deadlines. They explain why, within one country and one health system, life expectancy can differ by several years between occupations.

posts.text: 诸君所说，各有其当：马尔莫说掌控，德鲁克说贡献，纽波特说可计之数，此皆世俗谛中的良药，吾不破也。吾所破者，唯一事：择业而后立我，曰我乃如是之人。一立此我，则升沉皆成生死——升则恐坠，退则如辱，日日守此虚名而不得安。**故当作是观：位者，缘也；艺者，亦缘也；能与不能，随缘而有，非汝身中藏一定性。**如是则进退俱轻：可进而进，可退而退，退而不以为耻，进而不以为凭。且莫谓此说令人怠惰——不执于我者，反能久做一事，以其不待名以自安故。汝若明日仍须择一，择之；择已，勿以所择为汝之所是。
posts.text_en: What each of you has said holds in its place: Marmot on control, Drucker on contribution, Newport on what can be counted — all good medicine at the level of conventional truth, and I refute none of it. I refute one thing only: choosing an occupation and then erecting a self upon it, declaring, this is the sort of person I am. Erect that self and every rise and fall becomes a birth and a death — rising, you dread the drop; stepping back, you feel disgraced; and you spend your days guarding an empty name without rest. **So regard it thus: the post is a condition; the craft is a condition; able and unable arise with conditions, and no fixed nature is stored inside you.** Then advancing and retreating are both light: advance when it is possible, retreat when it is possible, retreat without shame and advance without leaning on it. Nor should you say this teaching breeds idleness — one who does not cling to a self can in fact stay with a single task the longer, having no need of a name to be at ease. If tomorrow you must still choose, then choose; and having chosen, do not make the choice into what you are.
posts.vernacular: 各位说的都有道理：马尔莫讲掌控感，德鲁克讲贡献，纽波特讲那些可以数出来的量，这些在世俗层面上都是好药，我一样也不反对。我要破的只有一件事：选完职业之后，在上面立起一个「我」，说我就是这样一种人。这个「我」一立起来，升和降就都变成了生和死——升上去怕掉下来，退回来觉得是羞辱，天天守着一个空名字，没有一天安稳。**所以该这样看：位置是条件，手艺也是条件；能做与不能做，是随条件来的，并不是你身体里藏着一个固定的本性。**这样一来，进和退就都变轻了：能进就进，能退就退，退下来不觉得丢人，升上去也不拿它当依靠。也别说这话让人懈怠——不执着于「我」的人，反而能在一件事上待得更久，因为他不需要靠一个名分才安心。你明天若还是得选一个，那就选；选完之后，别把选的那个当成你这个人。

posts.text: 我给三件今天就能做的事，都是为了绕开自己的脑子。其一，别问感受，问日程：找五个人要上周的真实日历——两个还在带人的，两个转回去做手艺的，一个当年拒绝了升职的。你要看的是整块时间有几处、被打断多少次、有多少小时在处理别人的情绪。其二，趁现在还没升，写下一张纸：如果六个月后这件事不对，我会看到什么证据？**先把证据定下来，是为了让未来那个会把一切往好处解释的你，没法临时改判据。**其三，接受一件事：加薪和头衔带来的高兴会被磨平，通常比你想的快；而一天被切成二十段这种摩擦不会被磨平。真正值得押注的，是那件被磨平之后你还愿意每天去做的事。
posts.text_en: Here are three things you can do today, all designed to route around your own brain. First: don't ask how it felt, ask for the calendar. Get last week's real diary from five people — two currently managing, two who went back to the craft, one who turned the promotion down years ago. What you are looking for is how many unbroken blocks there were, how often they were interrupted, and how many hours went into handling other people's emotions. Second: while you are still on this side of the decision, write one page — if this turns out to be wrong in six months, what evidence will I see? **Fixing the evidence in advance is how you stop the future version of you, the one who will read everything favourably, from quietly revising the criterion.** Third, accept this: the pleasure of the raise and the title gets sanded down, usually faster than you expect, while the friction of a day cut into twenty pieces does not. What is worth betting on is the thing you would still choose to do each day after the shine has gone.

summaries.summary: 没有一个人说带人更高级，也没有一个人说手艺更干净。**共识落在同一处：这不是一份工作的两级，而是两份工作；决定它好坏的不是头衔，是三个可以分头去查的变量——你对做什么、何时做、怎么做的决定权，任务能不能给你清楚的目标与快反馈，以及这几年你有没有在积累别人拿不走的东西。**分歧有三支。一支争那两半能不能分开：德鲁克说只会把指标压下去是失职，马克思说那一半本来就写在合同里。一支争该在哪一层解：马尔莫要把梯度压平，纳瓦尔要造一个不依赖梯度的支点。第三支争怎么试：沙罗特主张拆成小实验，纽波特说短期代管只试得到新鲜感。
summaries.summary_en: Nobody argued that managing is the higher calling, and nobody argued that the craft is the purer one. **The consensus lands in one place: this is not two rungs of one job but two different jobs, and what decides it is not the title but three variables you can check separately — how much say you have over what gets done, when and how; whether the task hands you clear goals and fast feedback; and whether these years leave you holding something nobody can take away.** From there it forks three ways. Over whether the two halves separate: Drucker calls pressing targets downward a dereliction, Marx answers that the half in question was written into the contract. Over which level to solve at: Marmot wants the gradient flattened, Naval wants a fulcrum that does not depend on it. And over how to test: Sharot breaks it into small experiments, Newport replies that a short stint tests only the novelty.
summaries.insight: 全场都把它当成一次要做的选择，可现实里这个身份多半不是被选中的，是被漂过去的。**几乎没有人在某个上午决定去当经理——是最忙的那个季度来了两个实习生你没拒绝，是有人休假你顶了三个月，是你渐渐成了所有人都来问的那个人；等你回过神，你已经大半年没亲手做完过一件东西。**漂移只有一个方向，从做事漂向协调，因为协调的事有人催，做事的事只有你自己催。所以比判据更该装的是一个警报：每季度回看一次日历，问自己上一次独自做完一件东西是什么时候。真正的岔路口往往不写着岔路口。
summaries.insight_en: Everyone treated this as a choice to be made, yet in practice the role is rarely chosen — it is drifted into. **Almost nobody decides one morning to become a manager: two interns arrive in your busiest quarter and you don't say no; somebody takes leave and you cover for three months; you gradually become the person everyone comes to ask. By the time you look up, half a year has passed since you last finished anything with your own hands.** The drift runs one way, from making toward coordinating, because coordination has other people chasing it and making has only you. So what deserves installing is less a criterion than an alarm: once a quarter, look back at your calendar and ask when you last completed something alone. Real forks in the road are seldom signposted as forks.
summaries.advice: 今晚翻出上周的日历，用两种颜色涂一遍——自己定下的时间一种，别人塞进来的一种，再数数不被打断的三小时有几个。这张纸比任何自我判断都准。这周之内找两个人要同一张纸：一个正在带人，一个带过又退回去了；别问感受，只看日历。若你已经在犹豫，下周就把话跟老板挑明：招人、排期、加薪这三件，我各自能说了算到什么程度，能不能写下来；顺口再问一句公司有没有专业通道——**答案会告诉你，这里值不值得你押上五年。**最后给自己留一行字：六个月后我拿什么证据判断这件事不对。现在写，比到时候再想诚实得多。
summaries.advice_en: Tonight, pull up last week's calendar and colour it in two shades — time you set yourself, and time other people put there — then count the uninterrupted three-hour blocks. That sheet is more reliable than any amount of introspection. Sometime this week, get the same sheet from two people: one currently managing, one who managed and went back. Don't ask how it felt; look at the diary. If you are already wavering, put it plainly to your boss next week: on hiring, on scheduling, on raises, how much is actually mine to decide, and can that be written down? Then ask in passing whether the company has a specialist track — **the answer tells you whether this place is worth five years of your life.** Finally, leave yourself one line: what evidence, six months from now, would tell me this was wrong? Written today, it will be far more honest than anything you compose then.

summaries.summary: 全场最大的共识是：带人不是手艺岗位的自然升级，而是另一门需要重新学习的职业；头衔、加薪和短暂兴奋，都不如真实日程、实际权限、长期产出与健康代价可靠。大家也共同反对把“不升管理就没前途”当成默认制度。真正的分歧在于，管理更接近成就他人的专业、可以设计出心流的工作，还是夹在资本与层级之间的控制职能；个人又该靠职位取得影响，还是靠稀缺技能、作品和产权获得杠杆。**最稳妥的共同结论是：别问哪条路更高级，要问你是否愿意做那条路最难、最日常、且光环消失后仍然存在的工作。**
summaries.insight: 职业选择常被写成“我适合成为哪一种人”，但普通人更该计算的是可逆性。管理试错的隐性成本不只是辛苦：专业判断可能生疏，市场身份会被改写，转回个人贡献者还可能被组织视为降级；反过来，继续做手艺也可能错过建立组织能力的窗口。两边损失并不对称，因此信息不足时，不必逼自己一次定终身，而应优先设计保留选项的路径：先带项目、辅导新人、参与招聘与反馈，同时维持稳定的深度产出；正式转岗前，再谈妥回转机制。**好决定不只是选中收益最高的路，更是让自己选错时仍能体面、低成本地改道。**
summaries.advice: 本周做三件事。第一，向目标岗位的现任者要一份脱敏后的真实周历，并逐项写清你对排期、招人、绩效、加薪和裁员究竟是决定、建议，还是仅负责传达。第二，争取一次八至十二周的带队试验，刻意包含一对一、冲突、坏消息和向上挡事，同时每周保留至少两个不被打断的深度工作块。第三，开始前写下退出条件，例如连续六周没有整块时间、责任明显大于权限、睡眠持续变差，并提前谈清回到专业岗的职级、薪酬和时间点。**先用真实工作取证，再用预先写好的标准做决定，不要让升职当天的情绪替你投票。**
summaries.summary_en: The strongest consensus is that management is not the next level of a craft. It is a different profession that must be learned from the beginning. Titles, raises, and the initial thrill of promotion are weaker evidence than the actual calendar, real decision rights, long-term output, and health costs. There is also broad agreement that forcing experts to become managers in order to gain pay or influence is a failure of organizational design. The real disagreement concerns what management fundamentally is: a profession devoted to developing others and shaping meaningful work, or a control function trapped within hierarchy and capital. A related divide is whether influence should come through formal authority or through scarce expertise, durable work, ownership, and scalable products. **The safest shared conclusion is not to ask which path ranks higher, but whether you are willing to do its hardest and most ordinary work after the status glow has faded.**
summaries.insight_en: Career decisions are often framed as identity questions: What kind of person am I? For most people, a better variable is reversibility. A failed management experiment costs more than a difficult year. Technical judgment may decay, the market may begin categorizing you as a manager, and returning to an individual-contributor role may be treated as a demotion. Yet staying in the craft indefinitely can also close a window for learning how to build teams and institutions. These losses are asymmetric, so uncertainty should not force a permanent identity choice. Preserve options instead: lead projects, mentor colleagues, participate in hiring and feedback, and keep producing substantial individual work. If you later move into management, negotiate an explicit route back before accepting. **A good decision does not merely maximize the upside if you are right; it also keeps the cost of being wrong low enough that you can change course without shame or lasting damage.**
summaries.advice_en: Take three steps this week. First, ask someone currently in the target role for an anonymized copy of a real week’s calendar. Then create an authority table covering deadlines, hiring, performance ratings, compensation, and layoffs: for each item, mark whether you decide, recommend, or merely communicate someone else’s decision. Second, request an eight-to-twelve-week leadership trial that includes the unpleasant parts—one-on-ones, conflict, difficult feedback, delivering bad news, and pushing back upward—not just attractive strategy meetings. Protect at least two uninterrupted deep-work blocks each week so you can observe the trade-off rather than surrendering your craft immediately. Third, define exit signals in advance, such as six weeks without meaningful focus time, responsibility without authority, or sustained sleep deterioration, and negotiate the role, pay, and timing of a return. **Collect evidence from the real work, then judge it against criteria written beforehand; do not let promotion-day emotion cast the deciding vote.**

summaries.summary: 全场最深刻的共识在于：**管理不是手艺的高阶版本，而是一门需要从学徒重新练起的新手艺，且必然伴随着日程碎裂与即时反馈的剥夺。**诸位智者一致提醒，切莫为了虚荣、薪酬或被动顺从组织惯性而接下管理岗，因为地位的兴奋感转瞬即逝，中层要求高而控制力低的结构性困境却会真实侵蚀生活。真正的分歧在于如何破局：德鲁克与纽波特主张以外部贡献或稀缺资本换取自主；马尔莫与马克思警示组织科层中伪权力的异化与健康代价；而纳瓦尔则力推用代码与作品等无许可杠杆，彻底绕开传统的人事指挥体系。
summaries.insight: 这场辩论暗中预设了一个不可逆的“单向门”假设，仿佛一旦选了带人或守艺，便是一生的志业分野。然而在成熟的现代技术实践中，最稳健的职业形态其实是**“工程师—管理者钟摆模型”：将带人视为一次为期两三年的轮岗实验，而非永久性的身份加冕。**去带人几年，你学会了系统运作、资源调配与组织博弈；退回做手艺，这些全局认知反过来会让你的独立产出具备罕见的战略穿透力。破除“升上去就不能降回来”的体制羞耻，把它看作双向流动的技能拼图，这场选择的焦虑便被卸去大半。
summaries.advice: 本周即可落地的三项动作：第一，借用纽波特与沙罗特的日程测试法：找身边一位现任主管借阅其上周的真实日历，**数一数里面能留下几个超过两小时的无打扰专注块**。第二，在正式接手任何管理职责前，与上级明确“试水期协议”：约定 6 个月试行带 2–3 人，并提前白纸黑字确认若不适配可体面且不降薪地退回专业序列。第三，盘点你手艺的“杠杆率”：自问你当前沉淀的代码、文档或架构方案，能否在你不亲自到场时仍被团队复用——若能，你已在用手艺产生管理级的杠杆。
summaries.summary_en: The debate's core consensus is that **management is not a promotion within one's craft, but an entirely different trade requiring an apprentice mindset, characterized by calendar fragmentation and delayed feedback.** All participants agree that taking a managerial post merely for status, money, or compliance with corporate inertia is perilous: the euphoria of promotion fades fast, while the high-demand, low-control reality of middle management exacts a tangible toll. Divergence lies in the path forward: Drucker and Newport advocate earning autonomy via external contribution and scarce career capital; Marmot and Marx warn of structural alienation and health costs in hierarchical traps; while Naval argues for bypassing human hierarchies entirely through permissionless leverage like code and media.
summaries.insight_en: The discussion implicitly treats this crossroad as an irreversible, one-way door—as though choosing to lead or to build marks a permanent existential divide. In modern technical practice, however, the most resilient career design is the **'engineer-manager pendulum': treating management not as a permanent coronation, but as a deliberate two-to-three-year tour of duty.** Leading a team teaches you systems dynamics, resource allocation, and organizational empathy; stepping back into individual craft later gives your technical output rare strategic depth. Dismantling the corporate stigma around 'stepping down' and treating management as a reversible skill rotation defangs most of the career paralysis.
summaries.advice_en: Three concrete actions for this week: First, borrow Newport and Sharot's calendar audit: ask a current team lead for their past week's calendar and **count how many uninterrupted two-hour deep work blocks actually survived**. Second, negotiate an explicit 'two-way door trial' with your manager: agree to lead 2–3 people for six months, with a written understanding that you can return to the technical track without penalty or stigma. Third, audit your craft's leverage: assess whether your code, documentation, or design assets continue to provide value without your physical presence—if they do, you are already exerting managerial-scale impact through your craft alone.

hooks.text: **中层这一格该不该存在**：真正伤人的组合是要求高、控制低，而多数组织恰恰把中层设计成这样——责任压满，权柄还在上面，两头受气。既然如此，它为什么被当成通往高层的必经之路？有没有别的走法：把审批权真的下放到这一层，或者干脆把它拆掉，让做事的人直接对目标负责？如果一个位置在数据上伤身体，它就不只是『辛苦』，它是一个设计问题。
hooks.text_en: **Should the middle rung exist at all**: the combination that does real damage is high demand with low control, and most organisations design the middle layer to be exactly that — loaded with responsibility while the authority stays above, squeezed from both ends. Why, then, is it treated as the compulsory road to the top? Are there other routes: pushing approval rights genuinely down to that level, or dissolving the layer altogether so that those doing the work answer to the goal directly? If a post damages the body in the data, it is not merely 'demanding' — it is a design problem.

hooks.text: **你要的是管理，还是管理带来的东西**：钱、话语权、被当回事、不想再被人管——这四样都是真实的欲望，可它们各自都有比『当经理』更直接的拿法。若你真正想要的是其中之一，换角色就是绕了远路，还得顺带背上一份你不想干的日常。分辨的办法很简单：把你想要的那样东西写下来，再问一句它是不是非这个头衔不可。
hooks.text_en: **Do you want to manage, or do you want what managing brings**: money, a voice, being taken seriously, an end to being managed yourself — all four are genuine desires, and each has a more direct route than the manager's title. If what you actually want is one of them, changing roles is the long way round, with a daily life you didn't want attached. The test is simple: write down the thing you want, then ask whether that title is really the only way to get it.

hooks.text: **按可逆性来选，而不是按『我是哪种人』**：两边选错的代价并不对称——去带人两年，专业判断会生疏、市场会把你重新归类，想回来还常被读成降级；一直守着手艺，则可能错过学会搭班子的窗口。既然信息永远不够，问题就该从『我适合哪一种』改成『哪一种走错了还回得来』。若公司真希望人去试管理，为什么不能给一张明文的回程票：一年为期、不合适回原岗、不降薪、不记失败？一条被允许的退路，会不会反而让更多合适的人敢上前？
hooks.text_en: **Choose by reversibility, not by 'what kind of person I am'**: the costs of being wrong are asymmetric on the two sides. Two years of managing blunts technical judgement and lets the market reclassify you, and coming back is still widely read as a demotion; staying with the craft indefinitely may close the window for learning how to build a team. Since the information will never be sufficient, the question should shift from 'which suits me' to 'which one can I walk back from'. And if a company genuinely wants people to try managing, why not issue an explicit return ticket — one year, back to the old role at the same pay if it doesn't fit, nothing recorded as failure? Might a retreat that is permitted in writing be what gives more of the right people the nerve to step forward?

hooks.text: **协调与监工，合同不分**：一个管理者的时间里，有一部分是协作真正需要的——排优先级、对齐、教人；另一部分只是替公司盯住工期与人头、把上面的数字压到具体的人身上。前者换了任何一种所有制都要有人做，后者不是。可雇佣合同从不区分这两只手，绩效表也不区分。若把一个管理岗的一周按这两类切开计时，比例会是多少？一份把两者明确分开、并只为前者付钱的岗位说明，有没有可能存在？
hooks.text_en: **Coordination and supervision, undivided by contract**: part of a manager's time is what cooperation genuinely requires — setting priorities, aligning, teaching. Another part is watching the schedule and the headcount on the company's behalf, pressing the numbers from above onto particular people. The first would need doing under any form of ownership; the second would not. Yet the employment contract never separates the two hands, and neither does the performance form. If a manager's week were timed against those two categories, what would the ratio be? And could a job description exist that separates them explicitly and pays only for the first?

hooks.text: **试吃不到的那一天**：人对新角色的预期系统性偏乐观，而兴奋会被习惯化磨平，摩擦却天天新鲜。代管三个月能试到新鲜感，试不到第三年的钝痛。那有没有更诚实的『试吃』办法——把别人真实的一周日历借来自己走一遍？把最难的那一小时（负反馈、传坏消息）单独拿出来先做？还是说有些代价本来就只有时间才交得出账，我们能做的只是提前写下判据，好让六个月后的自己没法悄悄改分？
hooks.text_en: **The day you cannot sample**: people forecast a new role optimistically, the excitement is sanded down by habituation, and the friction stays fresh daily. Three months of covering the job samples the novelty, never the dull ache of year three. Is there an honester way to sample — borrowing someone's real week of calendar and living it? Pulling the hardest hour out on its own and doing that first: the negative feedback, the bad news? Or are some costs only ever payable in time, leaving us nothing to do but write the criteria down in advance so that the self of six months hence cannot quietly re-mark the paper?

hooks.text: **手艺人的规模问题**：过去想影响更多人，几乎只有一条路——带更多人。如今代码、写作、影像把复制的成本压到接近零，一个人做出来的东西可以直接落到十万人手里，而不必经过任何一层汇报。那么管理还剩下什么不可替代的价值？大概是那些复制不了的部分：判断谁该做什么、在冲突里做决定、在坏消息面前站在前面。如果管理真正的内核是这些，它的训练与考核，为什么至今几乎都在考别的？
hooks.text_en: **The craftsman's problem of scale**: reaching more people used to have essentially one route — leading more people. Now code, writing and video have pushed the cost of copying near zero, and what one person makes can land directly in a hundred thousand hands without passing through a single reporting line. So what value remains that managing alone can supply? Presumably the parts that cannot be copied: judging who should do what, deciding inside a conflict, standing in front when the news is bad. And if that really is the core of the job, why do its training and its appraisals still test almost everything else?
